title: Theorem 3.13 (Brascamp–Lieb inequality) of arXiv:2405.06616: Fast Mixing in Sparse Random Ising Models
body: [Theorem 3.13 (Brascamp–Lieb inequality) of arXiv:2405.06616, 'Fast Mixing in Sparse Random Ising Models'] For any distribution with density ν ∝exp(−V) for some V : Rn →R, if there is a matrix Γ ≻0 such that ∇2V(z) ⪰Γ uniformly, then Cov(ν) ⪯Γ−1. Using the Hubbard-Stratonovich transform with the Brascamp-Lieb inequality allows us to bound covariances using the following lemma.

title: Tensorization (Subadditivity) of Entropy
body:
Let X_1, ..., X_n be independent random variables and let Z = f(X_1, ..., X_n) be a nonnegative random variable with E[Z log Z] finite. Write Ent(Z) = E[Z log Z] - E[Z] log E[Z] and let Ent^{(i)}(Z) denote the same functional computed with respect to X_i alone, with the other coordinates held fixed. Then Ent(Z) <= sum_{i=1}^n E[ Ent^{(i)}(Z) ]. The same statement with variance in place of entropy is the Efron-Stein inequality, and the two are the p = 2 and p = 1 members of a family of phi-entropies that all tensorize. Tensorization is what converts a ONE-DIMENSIONAL functional inequality into an n-dimensional one with no loss of constant: if each coordinate's law satisfies a logarithmic Sobolev inequality with constant C, then the product law satisfies it with the SAME constant C, independent of n. That dimension-free feature is the whole reason the entropy method produces concentration bounds that do not degrade as n grows. Independence of the coordinates is essential. [standard; e.g. Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 4.10 and Section 4.1]
X_1, ..., X_n independent
Z = f(X) nonnegative with E[Z log Z] finite

metadata.proof_text: Use the variational (duality) formula for entropy: for Z >= 0 with E[Z log Z] finite, Ent(Z) = sup { E[Z U] : E[e^U] <= 1 }, the supremum attained at U = log Z - log E[Z] on {Z > 0}. Fix any U with E[e^U] <= 1 and let E_i denote conditional expectation given X_1, ..., X_i, with E_0 = E and E_n e^U = e^U. Telescope the exponential rather than U itself: e^U = E[e^U] * prod_{i=1}^n ( E_i e^U / E_{i-1} e^U ), so with U_i = log E_i e^U - log E_{i-1} e^U one has U = log E[e^U] + sum_i U_i <= sum_i U_i, because log E[e^U] <= 0. Hence E[Z U] <= sum_i E[Z U_i]. Now condition on X^{(i)} = (X_j)_{j != i}. By independence, E_{i-1} e^U is a function of X_1, ..., X_{i-1} alone, hence fixed given X^{(i)}, and averaging E_i e^U over X_i with the other coordinates fixed returns E_{i-1} e^U, so E[ e^{U_i} | X^{(i)} ] = 1. The one-variable duality formula, applied in the variable X_i with the others held fixed, then gives E[ Z U_i | X^{(i)} ] <= Ent^{(i)}(Z). Taking expectations and summing over i, E[Z U] <= sum_i E[ Ent^{(i)}(Z) ]; the supremum over admissible U is Ent(Z), which proves the inequality. (The earlier draft telescoped U linearly as E_i U - E_{i-1} U and claimed the conditional normalisation E[e^{U_i} | others] <= 1 by Jensen; that step does not hold, and the log-telescoping above is the standard repair - Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, proof of Theorem 4.10.)
